newsitem.title: USA: Measure may slash Calif. local gov't revs - report.
newsitem.headline: Measure may slash Calif. local gov't revs - report.

text.p: A tax initiative approved by California voters in November could deprive local governments of up to five percent of their local revenues, or up to $2.5 billion, a state report concluded.

California local governments raise more than $50 billion annually from taxes, assessments and fees. Most of these local revenues are not affected directly by Proposition 218, according to a report by the Legislative Analyst's Office.
The report concluded, however, that the constitutional initiative could cause up to a five percent annual decrease in these local government revenues, equivalent to $2.5 billion.

"The five percent figure is really the outer boundary, the worst case scenario," said Marianne O'Malley, the report's author. "Many local governments will not be significantly affected. Some, on the other hand, should be very worried."

The intent of Proposition 218 is to ensure that all taxes and most charges on property owners are subject to voter approval. It applies to California's nearly 7,000 cities, counties, special districts, schools, community college districts, redevelopment agencies and regional organizations.
The fiscal impact of Proposition 218 will begin almost immediately, the Legislative Analyst said in the report.

"Within eight months of Proposition 218's passage, local governments will need to reduce or eliminate certain existing assessments and fees to meet the measure's requirements," the Legislative Analyst said.
The Legislative Analyst estimated earlier this year that these action would reduce local government revenues by at least $100 million in 1997-1998.

Since the measure also requires local governments to place before the voters certain existing assessments and taxes, local governments could experience additional revenue losses, potentially exceeding $100 million annually, it said.
Since its passage last month, Proposition 218 has drawn considerable fire from local government officials throughout California and municipal analysts across the country.
The Los Angeles City Council recently voted to sue over the measure.
Major U.S. credit rating agencies have responded to the measure's passage by downgrading the debt of the cities of Los Angeles and San Diego.
The California Legislative Analyst's Office provides analysis and non-partisan advice to the state Legislature on fiscal and policy issues.
